title: ElasticMM: Efficient Multimodal LLMs Serving with Elastic Multimodal Paral

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract versus Introduction, Section 4.2, and Conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims ElasticMM reduces TTFT by "up to 6.8×" and achieves "5.1–7.2× higher throughput." The Introduction contribution list, Section 4.2, and Conclusion instead report at most 4.2× TTFT reduction and 3.2–4.5× throughput over vLLM. No experiment elsewhere reports the abstract's 6.8× or 5.1–7.2× values.

The displayed values and parenthetical multipliers are mathematically incompatible. For Qwen, vLLM is shown as approximately 250 QPM at SLO 1.0 and DistServe as approximately 450 QPM, labeled "4.5×"; 450/250 = 1.8, not 4.5. For Llama, vLLM is approximately 300 and DistServe approximately 450, labeled "3.2×"; 450/300 = 1.5, not 3.2. The table also associates later ElasticMM values with SLO scales but provides no corresponding baseline values at those scales from which its multipliers could be calculated.

The text says ElasticMM delivers up to 4.5× and 3.2× higher throughput than vLLM and up to 2.3× higher throughput than DistServe. The Figure 6 numbers as presented do not support these comparisons: at the only directly comparable shown SLO 1.0 values, DistServe—not ElasticMM—is displayed, and its ratios to vLLM are only 1.8× (450/250) and 1.5× (450/300).

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 Metrics and Section 4.2 Input Latency
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines normalized input latency as "average prefill time divided by input length" but repeatedly equates this quantity with TTFT. TTFT, including in the paper's own Figure 1 discussion, includes image preprocessing, image encoding, LLM prefill, and ordinarily queueing/first-token generation effects. A prefill-only normalized metric cannot be called TTFT, particularly when the claimed primary optimization is non-blocking image encoding.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, definition and Eq. (1) for burst tolerance
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The prose defines burst tolerance as "the difference between peak load and idle capacity normalized by total instances," but Eq. (1) defines bt(i) as N_i^peak / N_i^avg, a ratio. These are different quantities, with different optimization behavior. The subsequent greedy allocation therefore lacks a consistent objective.

The migration overhead M(e_max) is an instance-level one-time cost, yet Eq. (2) adds M(e_max) once for every request r in B_d: Σ_r [M(e_max)+...]/r.output_len. This makes the same single migration cost grow with the number of decoding requests and mixes it with per-token latency terms. No derivation justifies this repeated charging, so the stated gain-versus-cost decision rule is not a valid accounting of the described operation.

The claimed proof of parallelism invariance is invalid. The system states it "prioritize[s] Data Parallelism," but Eq. (13) treats data parallelism as partitioning a single image i into i_1,...,i_n, independently computing g_E^j(i_j), and gathering the results. Data parallelism replicates a model and partitions requests/batches, not a single transformer's input computation; independently encoding image partitions is generally not equivalent because vision transformers contain global attention. If a single request is partitioned across devices, that is model/sequence parallelism and requires communication that the equation omits. Thus Eqs. (12)–(16) do not establish invariance under the claimed elastic parallelism changes.

The numerical-stability argument falsely states that fp16 differences are approximately 10^-7. FP16 has roughly 10 bits of significand precision, with unit roundoff on the order of 10^-4 to 10^-3 near one, not 10^-7. Moreover, no universal bound of |Δp| < 10^-7 follows from deterministic reductions or mixed precision, and argmax can change whenever logits are sufficiently close; calling this "statistically negligible" is not a proof.

The proof asserts implementation guarantees not described in the implementation: deterministic CUDA operations, fixed random seeds across instances, identical floating-point settings, deterministic serialization/deserialization with checksum verification, and exact integrity checking for every migration. Appendix A describes NCCL communication and CUDA streams but does not specify these mechanisms. NCCL transfer/checksums alone do not guarantee identical floating-point results across changed parallel decompositions. Therefore the claimed formal guarantee of bit-identical inference is unsupported by the described system.

The paper identifies the evaluated model as LLaMA-3.2-Vision-11B and cites [21], but [21] is titled "Llama Guard 3 Vision: Safeguarding human-AI image understanding conversations," not the Llama 3.2 Vision model paper. It likewise calls the model Qwen2.5-VL-7B while citation [29] is "Qwen2-VL: Enhancing vision-language model's perception of the world at any resolution," not Qwen2.5-VL. These are materially different model releases and cannot serve as the stated model citations without correction.
Reference [55] is Dao's "FlashAttention-2: Faster attention with better parallelism and work partitioning," not Flash-Decoding. The text misidentifies the cited work.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5, claim "Zhang et al. [61] proposed a similar two-tier separation in 2024"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The reference list ends at [60]. There is no reference [61], so this prior-work attribution is unverifiable and the claim cannot be properly cited as written.

The paper claims applicability to "all MLLM architectures, including cross-attention, prefix-tuning, and adapter-based models" and later claims SLO compliance "under all workload conditions." The reported evaluation covers only two models, two datasets, a single eight-GPU workstation, and synthetic Poisson arrivals supplemented by unspecified traces. It presents no prefix-tuned or adapter-based model evaluation, no multi-node evaluation, and no evidence for all workload conditions. These universal claims substantially exceed the reported evidence.

The conclusion calls ElasticMM "a complete solution to the multimodal serving problem with no significant limitations or risks," while immediately acknowledging that multi-node deployment is unstudied and introduces important communication and parallelism-search challenges. The system was evaluated only on one workstation and two models, so the claim of no significant limitations directly overstates the demonstrated scope.
